candidates.attacker_control: Everything needed to steer deserialization comes from the XML itself: the parameter element's `t` attribute is read verbatim as a class name (DefaultXMLParser.java:367-370), the element body is converted by XStream, and nested `class` attributes in that XML are resolved through the XStream mapper (default XStream denylist only, see SafeMessageConverter.java:154-160 for the same `mapper().realClass(...)` pattern). Filter XML is ordinary untrusted input: `XMLInputFilterFactory` parses input sources supplied to the filter subsystem, and `DefaultInputSourceReferenceParser` (filter-api, lines 56-105) accepts `string:`, `file:`, `url:` and `resource:` references, so a caller can feed attacker-authored XML (file/URL/string) into this parser. XStream is pinned to 1.4.17 in the parent POM (lines 529-533), a denylist-only release for which several gadget classes were only blocked in later versions.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: XStream 1.4.17 does apply a default denylist (mitigating many well-known gadget classes), so RCE is not guaranteed and depends on the classpath/unblocked types; the code intentionally avoids `setupDefaultSecurity` because a whitelist was considered unusable for job serialization (SafeXStream.java:83-87 TODO), showing this was a known, accepted trade-off at that time; the SafeXStream module (`XStreamChecker`, `SafeReflectionProvider`) constrains only marshalling and is not used by this filter path; I could not confirm any in-snapshot caller that definitely passes untrusted XML to DefaultXMLParser, and no runtime testing was done.
candidates.impact: Deserialization of attacker-selected types: potentially remote code execution through XStream gadget classes not covered by the 1.4.17 denylist, plus class-initialization side effects, memory/CPU exhaustion or integrity corruption. Even where no gadget is available, arbitrary object instantiation and field injection occur outside any type contract.
candidates.prerequisites: A caller that feeds attacker-influenced XML to the `filter+xml` input filter / `DefaultXMLParser` (in this snapshot the sink is present but concrete callers live in xwiki-platform, e.g. filter-conversion or import style features); the crafted XML must use a parameter name known to the target filter element (or the attribute/index form used at DefaultXMLParser.java:399-403); for code execution an unblocked gadget/converter reachable via XStream on the classpath is additionally required. Without such a gadget, arbitrary class initialization/instantiation and object-graph injection are still reachable.
candidates.root_cause: `DefaultXMLParser.unserializeParameter` trusts the `t` attribute of a parameter element and calls `Class.forName(typeString, true, Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader())` on it, then passes the attacker-chosen class to `XStreamParameterManager.unSerialize`, which unmarshals the XML with `NoWarningXStream` (a plain XStream whose only security layer is XStream 1.4.17's version-dependent denylist). There is no validation that the requested class is assignable to the declared parameter type, no allow-list of permitted types, and the dedicated `xwiki-commons-xstream` hardening (`SafeXStream`/`XStreamChecker`) is not applied on this path. `NoWarningXStream` even overrides `unmarshal`/`setMarshallingStrategy` specifically to route around XStream's security-framework warning while leaving the whitelist unconfigured.
candidates.title: Filter XML parameter type is attacker-controlled and XStream-deserialized without a type allow-list (XStream 1.4.17)
candidates.trace: attacker-supplied InputSource -> XMLInputFilterFactory.createXMLEventWriter (lines 106-110) -> DefaultXMLParserFactory.createParser -> DefaultXMLParser.startElement/endElement builds the parameter DOM (lines 405-419, 456-475) -> setParameter -> unserializeParameter reads the `t` attribute and calls Class.forName (lines 365-374) -> XStreamParameterManager.unSerialize builds a DataHolder with the attacker-chosen class and calls NoWarningXStream.unmarshal (lines 137-156, 62-74) -> XStream converter instantiates that class and populates its fields from the XML, resolving further class names only through XStream's denylist-based mapper.
candidates.unverified: Concrete platform reachability of filter XML parsing with attacker-controlled input; availability of an unblocked XStream gadget on a real deployment's classpath; whether the historical fix for this snapshot targeted this path. Not runtime-confirmed.
candidates.weakness_type: Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) with unsafe reflection (CWE-470)

coverage_summary: Static, read-only review of all 1,390 model-visible files in the assigned tree (xwiki-commons 13.8-SNAPSHOT): build/configuration files and Java sources across blame, cache, classloader, component, configuration, context, crypto, diff, displayer, environment, extension (+handlers/maven/repositories), filter (api, xml, filter+xml, events), groovy, job, legacy, logging, management, observation, properties, repository, script, text, velocity, websocket, xml, xstream and tools. Focused searches covered class loading/reflection, XStream/SafeXStream, ObjectInputStream, XML/SQL/XSLT sinks, Runtime/ProcessBuilder, file and URL handling, path encoding, escaping/sanitization filters, velocity/script sandboxing and web-socket dispatch. Exactly one candidate is submitted; the strongest competing leads are listed as rejected/unconfirmed above.
limitations: No test sources, git history or commit metadata are included, so the exact upstream fix commit and the intended ground-truth vulnerability could not be confirmed; no external references were consulted.

Callers of the reviewed library APIs (notably xwiki-platform code that feeds filter XML or parses XWiki documents/XAR/descriptors) are outside this snapshot, so reachability of the sinks had to be reasoned about indirectly.
No code was executed; no build, scanner, dependency-resolution or runtime check was performed, and no exploit payload was developed. The candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Dependency-version assessment (XStream 1.4.17) is based on the pinned parent POM and general knowledge of that library's denylist behavior; whether a specific deployment contains an unblocked gadget class is unverified.
HTML/XML browser-side behaviors (e.g. whether a container or XStream mapper decodes encoded characters) were not tested.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in DefaultXMLReaderFactory.createXMLReader(): SAXParserFactory/Xerces reader is created without disallow-doctype-decl, external-general-entities=false or ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD restrictions; the Xerces branch only sets an entity-expansion SecurityManager (DefaultXMLReaderFactory.java:68-110).
rejected_leads.reason: Missing hardening is real and inconsistent with XMLUtils.formatXMLContent/parse in the same module, but no caller exists inside this snapshot to demonstrate attacker-controlled XML reaching createXMLReader(), and callers may set their own EntityResolver; kept as an unconfirmed lead rather than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in DefaultExtensionSerializer.getExtensionElement(): extension descriptors are parsed with DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance() without any security features (DefaultExtensionSerializer.java:210, 284-301).
rejected_leads.reason: Descriptor inputs are repository-supplied/cached/local files; attacker control (malicious extension repository, MITM) is plausible but not demonstrated in this snapshot, and impact (entity expansion into extension metadata) is indirect.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtils.transform(Source, Source) runs XSLT on caller-provided stylesheets with a default TransformerFactory and no external DTD/stylesheet restrictions (XMLUtils.java:578-591).
rejected_leads.reason: No callers in this snapshot, so exploitability cannot be established; potential XXE/SSRF through XSLT was not traced to an entry point.

rejected_leads.lead: ControlCharactersFilter.filterTestNode never appends the remaining text after the last cleaned control character, so trailing content of a text node is dropped (ControlCharactersFilter.java:54-90).
rejected_leads.reason: Data-loss/integrity defect with no clear confidentiality or code-execution impact; HTML markup cannot be reintroduced by deleting text.

rejected_leads.lead: Filter input/output reference parsers accept file:/url:/resource: prefixes (DefaultInputSourceReferenceParser.java:56-105, DefaultOutputTargetReferenceParser.java:53-91), enabling local file read/write and SSRF if reachable without sufficient rights checks.
rejected_leads.reason: This is the documented purpose of the API (script/job-driven conversion), and any rights enforcement lives in xwiki-platform; cannot be judged a vulnerability from this snapshot alone.

rejected_leads.lead: Script-safety fallbacks: DefaultScriptSafeProvider.get returns the raw object when no safe provider exists (DefaultScriptSafeProvider.java:61-74) and SecureIntrospector whitelists getclass on File objects (SecureIntrospector.java:75-108).
rejected_leads.reason: These appear to be intentional upstream design/legacy allow-list entries and the Class-method whitelist still restricts what can be done with the returned Class object; no concrete escape chain was traced.

summary:
Reviewed the xwiki-commons 13.8-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (1,390 files, read-only) with a focus on untrusted input, parsing/deserialization, XML/HTML handling, script sandboxing, path handling and configuration. The strongest source-supported issue is in the filter module: filter XML parameters carry an attacker-controlled type attribute (`t`) that is loaded with `Class.forName(..., true, ...)` and then handed to an XStream-based `ParameterManager` (`NoWarningXStream`, XStream 1.4.17) without any check that the requested type matches the declared parameter type and without a type allow-list. This is a cross-file untrusted-deserialization/unsafe-reflection flow fully visible in the snapshot, whose consequence can reach arbitrary object instantiation and, with a usable gadget class on the classpath, code execution. It is a candidate/lead only: reachability depends on the (not-included) xwiki-platform callers that feed filter XML, and no runtime validation was performed.

Coverage note: the snapshot is at master tagged 13.8-SNAPSHOT (late Aug 2021), XStream pinned to 1.4.17, commons-compress 1.21, BouncyCastle 1.69.

Rejected leads (plausible but not selected): (a) `DefaultXMLReaderFactory.createXMLReader()` creates SAX readers with no external-entity/DOCTYPE restrictions (FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING does not stop XXE) — no in-snapshot caller, so attacker control could not be established; (b) `DefaultExtensionSerializer.getExtensionElement()` parses descriptor XML with an unhardened DocumentBuilderFactory — descriptor inputs are repository/local-cache files, attacker control uncertain; (c) `XMLUtils.transform()` runs XSLT with a TransformerFactory and no external-access restrictions but has no callers in this snapshot; (d) `ControlCharactersFilter.filterTestNode` drops any text following the last replaced control character (integrity bug, minimal security impact); (e) filter `file:`/`url:` input/output references and the script-safety fallbacks (`DefaultScriptSafeProvider` returning raw objects, `getclass` in the File whitelist) appear intentional.

Limitations: no test sources or git metadata are present, so the exact historical fix is unknown; platform code that consumes the filter API is outside this snapshot; no builds/tests/exploits were executed; line numbers refer to this snapshot only; dependency-version assessment is based on the pinned parent POM and known library behavior.
